article_title: Promising Models for Preparing a Diverse, High-Quality Early Childhood Workforce
citation: Gardner, M., Melnick, H., Meloy, B., & Barajas, J. (2019). Promising models for preparing a diverse, high-quality early childhood workforce. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/preparing-diverse-high-quality-early-childhood-workforce
title: Family Child Care Apprenticeship: job-embedded pathway to Child Development Permits for home-based providers
description: The FCC Apprenticeship is a pilot program implemented by the SEIU Educator Training Center with partners at four California sites, designed for licensed family child care providers. It pairs accessible college coursework with on-the-job training: "Apprentices enroll in college courses that are conveniently offered during evening hours at community sites, in partnership with local community colleges." Apprentices receive home-visit coaching, site-coordinator advising, cohorts of 25 peers, wage enhancements from $100 to $500 per month, and stipends covering tuition, books, a laptop, and fees, making coursework free.
requirements: Partnership among a union educator training center, employers, child care resource and referral agencies, community colleges, and funders to deliver coursework, coaching, and financial supports
constraints: Designed for licensed family child care providers who work independently, a segment whose earnings are very low
target_learners: Current licensed family child care providers, predominantly low-income women of color
target_learning_goals: Child development knowledge and skills for early childhood teaching; attainment of California Child Development Permits
examples: In the FCC program's 2-year existence, 95 apprentices have earned new permits.
key_sources: Gardner, M., Melnick, H., Meloy, B., & Barajas, J. (2019). Promising models for preparing a diverse, high-quality early childhood workforce. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/preparing-diverse-high-quality-early-childhood-workforce

article_title: Transforming common-sense beliefs into Newtonian thinking through Just-In-Time Teaching
citation: S. P. Formica, J. L. Easley, and M. C. Spraker. (2010). Transforming common-sense beliefs into Newtonian thinking through Just-In-Time Teaching. Phys. Rev. ST Phys. Educ. Res. 6(2), 020106. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevSTPER.6.020106
title: Force Concept Inventory pretest/post-test protocol for measuring Newtonian conceptual gains in introductory physics
description: In this study the Force Concept Inventory (FCI) served as both pretest and post-test for examining 222 students in introductory physics courses taught by traditional lecture or Just-in-Time Teaching over five semesters. It provided both the overall normalized-gain comparison and the restricted Newton's Third Law item analysis, making it the measurement backbone of the study's instructional comparison.
requirements: Must be administered before and after instruction to compute gains
constraints: As used here, it measures understanding of Newtonian concepts in introductory physics courses
target_learning_goals: understanding Newtonian concepts such as Newton's Third Law
examples: The FCI was administered as a pretest and a post-test to 222 students across five semesters at North Georgia College & State University
key_sources: S. P. Formica, J. L. Easley, and M. C. Spraker. (2010). Transforming common-sense beliefs into Newtonian thinking through Just-In-Time Teaching. Phys. Rev. ST Phys. Educ. Res. 6(2), 020106. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevSTPER.6.020106

article_title: Systematic evaluation of the teaching effectiveness of flipped classroom mode in undergraduate preventive medicine courses in China.
citation: Zheng Hui, Ouyang Yun, Zeng Yifei, He Xinyu, Song Liping, Yu Xiangyuan. (2026). Systematic evaluation of the teaching effectiveness of flipped classroom mode in undergraduate preventive medicine courses in China. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1896815
title: Flipped classroom as an inversion of knowledge delivery explained via zone of proximal development and cognitive-process staging
description: The article describes the flipped classroom as "a blended learning model that inverts the traditional teaching process" in which knowledge delivery shifts to before class and classroom time is used for interaction, case discussion, and problem-solving. It explains the observed advantages through the "zone of proximal development" theory: lower-order cognitive processes occur before class and higher-order processes (analyzing, synthesizing, evaluating, creating) occur in class, "thereby achieving knowledge internalization and transfer". This is the framework the authors use to interpret their pooled results.
requirements: Students independently acquire content before class via activities such as watching instructional videos and reading literature
constraints: The authors note it is difficult to fully account for variability arising from differences in teaching implementation even under a random-effects model
target_learners: undergraduate medical and preventive medicine students in China
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge in preventive medicine courses
examples: Included trials implemented FC variants such as FC + PBL, FC + MOOC, and FC + micro-lecture videos in epidemiology, health statistics, and environmental hygiene courses
key_sources: Zheng Hui, Ouyang Yun, Zeng Yifei, He Xinyu, Song Liping, Yu Xiangyuan. (2026). Systematic evaluation of the teaching effectiveness of flipped classroom mode in undergraduate preventive medicine courses in China. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1896815

article_title: The Effect of Flipped Classroom Instruction in Writing: A Case Study with Iraqi EFL Learners
citation: Ramyar O. Qader and Fadime Yalcin Arslan. (2019). THE EFFECT OF FLIPPED CLASSROOM INSTRUCTION IN WRITING: A CASE STUDY WITH IRAQI EFL LEARNERS. Teaching English with Technology, 19(1), 36-55. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: Flipped writing course pattern: pre-class videos plus in-class collaborative practice
description: The article's FCI program had students preview instructional videos before class and spend class time on activities, group work, and pair work with the instructor present, rather than attending lectures. Videos were uploaded to a closed Facebook Social Media Community, with flash drives and DVDs available for students without internet. The same teaching schedule, textbook, and content were used for both groups.
requirements: Prepared videos accessible outside class, including offline alternatives for students without internet
Same instructor and materials across compared groups
constraints: Slow internet connection and video quality were reported problems in the Iraqi setting
target_learning_goals: paragraph writing: topic sentence, supporting and concluding sentences, unity and coherence
examples: Students viewed created videos through YouTube educational channels and a closed Facebook group, then practised via realistic applications such as group and pair work in class
key_sources: Ramyar O. Qader and Fadime Yalcin Arslan. (2019). THE EFFECT OF FLIPPED CLASSROOM INSTRUCTION IN WRITING: A CASE STUDY WITH IRAQI EFL LEARNERS. Teaching English with Technology, 19(1), 36-55. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1204642

article_title: The Effect of Flipped Classroom Strategy Using Blackboard Mash-Up Tools in Enhancing Achievement and Self-Regulated Learning Skills of University Students
citation: El-Senousy, H. & Alquda, J. (2017). The effect of Flipped Classroom Strategy using Blackboard Mash-Up Tools in enhancing achievement and Self–Regulated Learning skills of university students. World Journal on Educational Technology: Current Issues, 9(3), 144-157. https://sproc.org/ojs/index.php/wjet
title: Two-phase flipped classroom pattern: online multimedia at home, collaborative problem-solving class activities with immediate feedback
description: The pattern splits learning between home and class: students first engage with online media (videos, presentations, readings) individually at home, then spend class time in collaborative interactive groups on problem-solving, exercises, discussion and evaluation with teacher and peer feedback. The article states "The FCRS allows the using of online identical learning videos, recorded lectures or readings, that save the class time for practicing on exercises or applications through active groups based on problem answering activities". In the study this was implemented for 8 weeks with prepared working papers during class time.
requirements: Carefully selected high-quality online videos fitting each lesson's content
Prepared working papers with tasks students achieve during class time
Flexibility for students to access course materials on several mobile devices
constraints: FCRS, like other instructional strategies, suits some topics, students, specializations, learning environments and periods more than others, so it should be applied in appropriate context
target_learning_goals: moving learning from recall and understanding toward applying, analyzing, evaluating and creating
examples: The experimental group watched Mashup multimedia at home and completed working papers of problem solving, interactive learning, and group discussion during class time, guided by the teacher.
key_sources: El-Senousy, H. & Alquda, J. (2017). The effect of Flipped Classroom Strategy using Blackboard Mash-Up Tools in enhancing achievement and Self–Regulated Learning skills of university students. World Journal on Educational Technology: Current Issues, 9(3), 144-157. https://sproc.org/ojs/index.php/wjet

article_title: Family caregiving competencies for level one nursing education.
citation: Hart, S. E., Sexson, K., Perkins, C., Zhao, H., Cowen, N., Seward, T., Davis, A., & Mongoven, J. (2025). Family caregiving competencies for level one nursing education. Journal of Professional Nursing, 59, 138-147. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.profnurs.2025.05.006
title: The Family Caregiving Competencies for Level One Nursing Education (FCG-C): a four-domain competency framework for prelicensure nursing education
description: The article introduces the FCG-C, a set of 19 entry-level competencies across four domains: The Nature of Family Caregiving, Family Caregiving Identification and Assessment, Providing Family-centered Care, and the Systems-based Context of Family Caregiving. The framework aims to prepare nursing students to "identify, value, integrate, and support family caregivers" in person-centered care teams. It was developed by a national consortium of nurse educators and crosswalked with the AACN Essentials (2021).
requirements: Developed through consortium consensus processes including document review, crosswalking with the AACN Essentials, and validity checks such as national dissemination, expert feedback, and a survey of nursing educators
constraints: Designed for level one (prelicensure) nursing education; the article notes the work did not include direct input from family caregivers, relying instead on organizations representing them
target_learning_goals: Identify, value, integrate, and support family caregivers in person-centered and family-centered healthcare teams
key_sources: Hart, S. E., Sexson, K., Perkins, C., Zhao, H., Cowen, N., Seward, T., Davis, A., & Mongoven, J. (2025). Family caregiving competencies for level one nursing education. Journal of Professional Nursing, 59, 138-147. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.profnurs.2025.05.006

article_title: Student Learning Performance and Satisfaction With a Flipped Classroom in Undergraduate Dental Pharmacology Education.
citation: Galvin Sheila, Lucitt Margaret. (2026). Student Learning Performance and Satisfaction With a Flipped Classroom in Undergraduate Dental Pharmacology Education. European Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.70062
title: Flipped classroom design for dental pharmacology: pre-class recorded lectures with embedded reflective questions plus periodic live review sessions
description: The article's FC implementation is a hybrid asynchronous design: voiceover lecture slides recorded on Panopto, averaging 40 minutes, released weekly via Blackboard Learn, each accompanied by lecture notes, textbook readings and clinical case scenarios with reflective questions. Live in-person classes with the course lecturer were scheduled every 3 weeks for "review and reflection of released content". Course lecture topics, scheduling and faculty were consistent across delivery modes.
requirements: Students engage with pre-class content before live sessions
Scheduling and timed release of content to avoid information overload
constraints: No defined structure to the FC exists, so educators implement models suited to their subject content
target_learners: undergraduate dental science students in year 3 of a 5-year degree program
examples: Recorded lectures averaged 40 min and were released weekly over 2 semesters; live review classes occurred every 3 weeks
key_sources: Galvin Sheila, Lucitt Margaret. (2026). Student Learning Performance and Satisfaction With a Flipped Classroom in Undergraduate Dental Pharmacology Education. European Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.70062

article_title: Student Learning Performance and Satisfaction With a Flipped Classroom in Undergraduate Dental Pharmacology Education.
citation: Galvin Sheila, Lucitt Margaret. (2026). Student Learning Performance and Satisfaction With a Flipped Classroom in Undergraduate Dental Pharmacology Education. European Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.70062
title: Successful flipped classroom implementation requires engagement supports: content timing, faculty development, infrastructure and student readiness
description: The article's discussion recommends that institutions adopting a flipped classroom attend to enabling conditions, because "the full effect of the FC educational benefits will only be realized if students engage with the content before class". It lists careful consideration of curriculum design, timing of content delivery, faculty development, willingness to adapt teaching methods, technological infrastructure investment, appropriate staff-to-student ratios during discussion sessions, and ensuring student readiness and active participation as essential components.
requirements: Student engagement with pre-class content
Investment in technological infrastructure
Managing appropriate staff-to-student ratios during discussion sessions
constraints: Benefits depend on student self-directed learning outside the classroom as well as in-class instructor interaction
examples: The authors suggest scheduling and timed release of content to avoid overburdening student workloads
key_sources: Galvin Sheila, Lucitt Margaret. (2026). Student Learning Performance and Satisfaction With a Flipped Classroom in Undergraduate Dental Pharmacology Education. European Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.70062

article_title: Enhancing rational prescribing skills in pharmacy students: a blended learning model of flipped classroom and think-pair-share for cardiovascular pharmacology.
citation: Amin Mahsa, Abedi Farshad, Norouzi Azam, Karimi Gholamreza. (2026). Enhancing rational prescribing skills in pharmacy students: a blended learning model of flipped classroom and think-pair-share for cardiovascular pharmacology. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09166-y
title: Four-phase blended FC/TPS design with authentic prescriptions and gamification
description: The article describes a blended learning intervention "structured into four sequential phases": pre-class self-study with digital materials and real de-identified prescriptions, a 30-minute interactive lecture, a 60-minute structured Think-Pair-Share session analyzing novel prescriptions, and a gamified motivation phase. Prescriptions were tiered into Basic, Intermediate, and Advanced difficulty by two clinical pharmacy faculty reviewers.
requirements: Access to a university LMS (Moodle) for pre-class materials
A database of real, de-identified prescriptions reviewed and tiered by clinical faculty
Instructor time for interactive lecture, TPS facilitation, and public point tracking
constraints: Implemented within a compulsory cardiovascular pharmacology module at one Iranian pharmacy school
Evaluated only at Kirkpatrick Level 1 in this pilot
target_learners: undergraduate pharmacy students in their fourth year
examples: Teams earned publicly tracked points for TPS participation, with the top team receiving a monetary prize and the 'Excellence in Cardiovascular Pharmacology' award
key_sources: Amin Mahsa, Abedi Farshad, Norouzi Azam, Karimi Gholamreza. (2026). Enhancing rational prescribing skills in pharmacy students: a blended learning model of flipped classroom and think-pair-share for cardiovascular pharmacology. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09166-y

article_title: Enhancing rational prescribing skills in pharmacy students: a blended learning model of flipped classroom and think-pair-share for cardiovascular pharmacology.
citation: Amin Mahsa, Abedi Farshad, Norouzi Azam, Karimi Gholamreza. (2026). Enhancing rational prescribing skills in pharmacy students: a blended learning model of flipped classroom and think-pair-share for cardiovascular pharmacology. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09166-y
title: Satisfaction survey instrument (8 items, 4-point scale, Cronbach's α = 0.79)
description: A study-specific satisfaction survey assessing Kirkpatrick Level 1 perceptions, developed through multi-stage validation: an initial 15-item pool reduced by expert panel review (CVI below 0.78 revised or eliminated) and think-aloud interviews with five students, yielding 8 items on a 4-point scale (Excellent, Good, Moderate, Low) with no neutral option. Pilot testing with 15 separate students gave a mean completion time of 7.2 minutes and "acceptable" internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.79).
requirements: Expert panel review of item relevance, clarity, and representativeness
Think-aloud interviews to identify ambiguous items
constraints: Developed specifically for this study and context; content validity process described but no external validation reported
target_learning_goals: assessing student perceptions of a blended learning intervention
key_sources: Amin Mahsa, Abedi Farshad, Norouzi Azam, Karimi Gholamreza. (2026). article_title: Development and evaluation of a literature seminar course based on flipped classroom and team-based learning in the graduate nursing curriculum.
citation: Qi Hong, Ban Jingjing, Wang Nana, Guo Huimin, Yang Yang, Tang Shan. (2026). Development and evaluation of a literature seminar course based on flipped classroom and team-based learning in the graduate nursing curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08823-6
title: FC-TBL literature seminar course design: pre-class preparation, in-class team application, and post-class reflection across thematic research units
description: The course is a core compulsory module (two credits, 40 contact hours) organized into ten thematic units aligned with nursing research types. Each four-hour unit follows an FC-TBL sequence: students complete assigned preparatory materials individually before class, then "worked in stable teams on structured application tasks" in class, producing shared products such as article critiques, concept maps, or evidence syntheses. After class, students write individual reflective summaries and revise presentations based on feedback, forming what the authors call "a closed-loop instructional process of knowledge acquisition, ability internalization, and cognitive development."
requirements: Students must have completed core graduate-level coursework in research methodology and evidence-based practice before enrollment, providing a foundation in research literacy.

Stable teams of 13–15 members each with elected leaders and assigned roles (literature retrieval, methodological analysis, concept mapping, presentation delivery, slide integration, feedback recording) to support coordinated collaboration.
Each group must select one paper from a Chinese core nursing journal and one from a high-impact SCI journal for comparative analysis and presentation.
constraints: Roles are used as an organizational scaffold rather than isolated task ownership to reduce the risk of fragmented work.
The intervention emphasized team-based inquiry and did not require each student to develop a complete individual research proposal.
target_learners: second-year master's nursing students (graduate nursing postgraduates)
target_learning_goals: research competence (problem identification, literature retrieval, research design, research practice, data processing, thesis writing)
examples: Students compared one paper from a Chinese core nursing journal with one from a high-impact SCI journal, conducted joint reading sessions, collaboratively constructed a conceptual framework map, and delivered 30–35 minute team presentations followed by cross-group discussion with instructor feedback.
key_sources: Qi Hong, Ban Jingjing, Wang Nana, Guo Huimin, Yang Yang, Tang Shan. (2026). Development and evaluation of a literature seminar course based on flipped classroom and team-based learning in the graduate nursing curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08823-6

article_title: Effectiveness of flipped classroom model in distance education: An experimental study in Turkish language course.
citation: Aslan Seda Aktı, Turgut Yigit Emrah, Ünlü Gökhan, Allison Jordan. (2025). Effectiveness of flipped classroom model in distance education: An experimental study in Turkish language course. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0335721
title: Flipped classroom implementation package for live online classes: short expert-reviewed videos, worksheets, and Zoom breakout-room cooperative learning
description: The article's experimental intervention consisted of researcher-produced pre-class materials and in-class collaborative sessions. For each of the learning outcomes the team prepared 6–7-minute narrated videos and worksheets: "The videos were created by taking screen recordings of narrated PowerPoint presentations prepared by the researcher and included audio narration." Materials were reviewed by two experts, shared weekly via Moodle, and preparation was monitored and prompted with reminders. During twice-weekly 45-minute Zoom sessions, "Breakout rooms were used for cooperative learning activities" with heterogeneously formed groups and teacher visits to guide discussion.
requirements: Students complete preparatory video watching and worksheets before each synchronous session, supported by LMS tracking and weekly reminders
constraints: Preparatory activities were not graded or formally assessed
The same package was designed for 15 learning outcomes in a single Turkish Language course over 12 weeks
target_learners: undergraduate students in a Turkish Language course
target_learning_goals: Turkish language grammar learning outcomes such as sentence types, subject and predicate identification
examples: Videos and worksheets were prepared for each of the 15 learning outcomes and evaluated by experts in instructional technologies and Turkish language education
key_sources: Aslan Seda Aktı, Turgut Yigit Emrah, Ünlü Gökhan, Allison Jordan. (2025). Effectiveness of flipped classroom model in distance education: An experimental study in Turkish language course. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0335721

article_title: Effectiveness of flipped classroom model in distance education: An experimental study in Turkish language course.
citation: Aslan Seda Aktı, Turgut Yigit Emrah, Ünlü Gökhan, Allison Jordan. (2025). Effectiveness of flipped classroom model in distance education: An experimental study in Turkish language course. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0335721
title: Embed explicit self-directed learning support and structured interaction protocols when implementing the flipped classroom in synchronous online settings
description: The article's authors recommend "incorporating supportive instructional designs that consider individual learner differences to enhance the effectiveness of FCM in synchronous online learning environments", and specifically suggest "integrating strategies aimed at fostering self-directed learning into the structure of the FCM". They also argue, from the Community of Inquiry framework, that the absence of structured interaction protocols may have limited deep engagement, so protocols such as peer assessment, rotating discussion leadership, or guided reflection should be built in.
requirements: Students' self-directed learning skills must be explicitly taught step-by-step rather than assumed
constraints: In this study's implementation, which lacked such supports, SLS and course interaction did not significantly improve
target_learners: undergraduate students in synchronous online courses
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning skills and meaningful course interaction in live online classes
examples: The article recommends future work on FCM implementations enriched with self-regulatory learning strategies, and discusses structured interaction protocols such as peer assessment, rotating discussion leadership, and guided reflection
key_sources: Aslan Seda Aktı, Turgut Yigit Emrah, Ünlü Gökhan, Allison Jordan. (2025). Effectiveness of flipped classroom model in distance education: An experimental study in Turkish language course. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0335721

article_title: Synergising flipped classroom and case-based learning in resource-intensive anatomy education in China: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Yao Qianyin, Zhu Peiyi, Zou Zixi, Cheng Yatao, Liang Yaojian, Huang Wenyu. (2025). Synergising flipped classroom and case-based learning in resource-intensive anatomy education in China: a quasi-experimental study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-102001
title: FCCL in-class session pattern: Q&A reinforcement, application analysis and clinical case analysis in small groups
description: The article's FCCL design organises each 90-minute flipped session for eight groups of eight students around three synergistic components. It reports: "the Q&A reinforced core anatomical knowledge, application exercises built interpretive and reasoning skills and case discussions integrated learning in a realistic clinical context." Sessions follow pre-class video viewing and a closed-book specimen quiz, with the instructor acting as facilitator and students writing reflective journals afterwards.
requirements: Students must watch the assigned pre-class videos and complete the pre-class specimen quiz before the session; the article states inadequate preparation would hinder benefiting from in-class activities.
constraints: The nervous system was excluded from the FC approach and taught traditionally due to its complexity.
target_learning_goals: systematic anatomy knowledge across nine organ systems
clinical reasoning connecting structure to practice
examples: Digestive tract chapter example: students discussed gastric feeding tube head positioning based on anatomical structure and analysed a gastric ulcer perforation case leading to partial gastrectomy.
key_sources: Yao Qianyin, Zhu Peiyi, Zou Zixi, Cheng Yatao, Liang Yaojian, Huang Wenyu. (2025). Synergising flipped classroom and case-based learning in resource-intensive anatomy education in China: a quasi-experimental study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-102001

article_title: First year nursing students' knowledge, skill levels and learning persistence in nursing practices: a comparison between classical lecture and flipped classroom.
citation: Özkan Çiğdem Gamze; Demırbağ Birsel Canan. (2025). First year nursing students’ knowledge, skill levels and learning persistence in nursing practices: a comparison between classical lecture and flipped classroom. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07574-0
title: FCM instructional material package: PowerPoint presentations, 2D/3D animations, and laboratory-shot skill videos
description: The researchers built a digital teaching package in which "FCM teaching material consists of PowerPoint presentations on four topics, two- and three-dimensional animations and videos of basic nursing skills". Presentations covered vital signs, nutrition, drug management and parenteral drug preparation; skill videos of 5 to 15 minutes were shot in the nursing skills laboratory as practical explanations of all process steps; contents were combined into lesson videos recorded in a virtual studio and shared via a Teaching Management System and WhatsApp one week before each lesson.
requirements: Materials must be made available to students one week before the lesson
Videos and animations must cover the process steps of the target nursing skills
target_learning_goals: pre-class acquisition of theoretical nursing knowledge
repeated exposure to skill demonstration steps before practice
examples: Lesson videos combined presentations with laboratory-shot videos and researcher-narrated animations
key_sources: Özkan Çiğdem Gamze; Demırbağ Birsel Canan. (2025). First year nursing students’ knowledge, skill levels and learning persistence in nursing practices: a comparison between classical lecture and flipped classroom. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07574-0

article_title: Application of a flipped classroom incorporating modified team-based learning in molecular biology laboratory teaching: a mixed methods study.
citation: Qu Meng, Hou Qinlong, Li Xushen, Yu Chunyan, Xia Jichen, Dong Zhiheng. (2024). Application of a flipped classroom incorporating modified team-based learning in molecular biology laboratory teaching: a mixed methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06450-7
title: FC-TBL laboratory course pattern: pre-class self-study with iRAT, in-class tRAT and team experiments, post-class discussion
description: This pattern organizes a laboratory course into three phases. Pre-class, students receive readings, videos, slides and guiding questions via an online platform and complete an Individual Readiness Assurance Test of "8–10 closed-book multiple-choice questions". In class, teams present consensus answers in a tRAT, discuss, then conduct experiments and answer "3–5 questions based on the 4 S principles (significant problem, same problem, specific choice, simultaneous response)". Post-class, students submit lab reports and join group discussions of at least 30 minutes.
requirements: An online platform for distributing pre-class resources and administering the iRAT within a specified time frame
Learning teams balanced by GPA and gender, of 6–7 students each
Identical lecture settings, instructors and materials across comparison groups
constraints: The article notes the absence of adaptive assessment mechanisms and low pre-class engagement as challenges flipped classrooms must address, which TBL components are intended to mitigate
examples: At Beihua University, 55 students in the FC-TBL group completed four weekly 180-minute sessions covering nucleic acid extraction, quantitative analysis, PCR and electrophoresis, with 100 minutes of in-class experimental activity per session.
key_sources: Qu Meng, Hou Qinlong, Li Xushen, Yu Chunyan, Xia Jichen, Dong Zhiheng. (2024). Application of a flipped classroom incorporating modified team-based learning in molecular biology laboratory teaching: a mixed methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06450-7

article_title: Effect of virtual case-based learning (CBL) using the flipped class and peer instruction on the motivation to learn basic sciences.
citation: Alizadeh M, Saramad A, Rafiepoor H, Taghvaei A, Rayati R, Sibevei S, Seyyedlar ZS, Peighambardoust S, Zomorrodi A, Taghavi AA. (2024). Effect of virtual case-based learning (CBL) using the flipped class and peer instruction on the motivation to learn basic sciences. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06229-w
title: Facilitated CBL virtual course (FCVC): three-day virtual case-based learning sessions with flipped classroom and peer instruction
description: The FCVC was an extra-curricular series of webinars in which students in teams of 5–7, each with a trained moderator, discussed clinical scenarios on the Big Blue Button platform. "Each virtual case-based discussion consisted of three phases and was completed in three days": Day 1 case discussion (60–90 min), Day 2 presentations and peer learning (60–120 min), Day 3 conclusion with questions and expert summary (~120 min). Thirty clinical scenarios were designed by basic scientists and clinical educators using David Cohen's twelve tips for writing a discussion case.
requirements: Trained moderators per team, facilitator training via workshop with group work, exercises and role play on facilitation skills
Clinical scenarios standardized using twelve tips from David Cohen and reviewed by five other teachers
constraints: Extra-curricular program at a single institution during the COVID-19 pandemic
target_learning_goals: understanding the importance and application of basic sciences in medicine
examples: Seven virtual CBL courses across cardiology, pulmonology, gastroenterology, endocrinology, nephrology and neurology
key_sources: Alizadeh M, Saramad A, Rafiepoor H, Taghvaei A, Rayati R, Sibevei S, Seyyedlar ZS, Peighambardoust S, Zomorrodi A, Taghavi AA. (2024). Effect of virtual case-based learning (CBL) using the flipped class and peer instruction on the motivation to learn basic sciences. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06229-w

article_title: Exploring the mediating effect of creativity on the relationship between family capital and academic achievement in geography.
citation: An Zhenni, Ge Jiahao, Xu Yanhua, Liang Xiaoyu, Zhang Jianzhen, Oubibi Mohamed. (2023). Exploring the mediating effect of creativity on the relationship between family capital and academic achievement in geography. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-48833-8
title: FCQ, Innovative Behavior Scale, and standardized geography achievement scale used as the measurement battery
description: The study used a four-section survey: demographics, a Family Capital Questionnaire adapted from the PISA 2018 Family Background Questionnaire covering parents' schooling, occupations and family assets, a nine-item Innovative Behavior Scale with idea generation, promotion and realization dimensions, and a standardized Academic Achievement in Geography Scale that maps six grade bands to points 1–6. Reliabilities were printed as "the Cronbach's alpha of the scale was 0.735" for FC, 0.901 for creativity, and 0.776 for achievement.
requirements: Participants completed the questionnaire within one week of the midterm so students could remember their geography scores
constraints: The FC questionnaire consists of six questions covering only three selected PISA dimensions
examples: Principal component analysis of standardized z-values of the six family-capital items was used to compute a household capital score
key_sources: An Zhenni, Ge Jiahao, Xu Yanhua, Liang Xiaoyu, Zhang Jianzhen, Oubibi Mohamed. (2023). Exploring the mediating effect of creativity on the relationship between family capital and academic achievement in geography. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-48833-8

article_title: Application of flipped classroom combined with case-based learning in Introduction to Environmental Health Science.
citation: Li You, Cao Liang, Zhang Huixia, Pang Weiyi, Sun Yan, Zhang Zhiyong. (2023). Application of flipped classroom combined with case-based learning in Introduction to Environmental Health Science. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2023.1264843
title: FC+CBL implementation of Introduction to Environmental Health Science for MPH at Guilin Medical University
description: A course-level implementation combining flipped classroom and case-based learning for a required MPH course. Classic cases in five content areas (environmental pollution, indoor air pollution, occupational poisoning or injury, food poisoning and transgenic food, social factors and health) were "sent to the students through QQ or the Rain class platform before class"; students worked in 3–4-person groups, analysed the case, made slides, and reported in class, followed by joint teacher–student analysis. Assessment combined daily performance (30%) and paper results (70%).
requirements: Students need pre-class access to cases via an online platform (QQ or Rain class) and time to prepare group presentations
Cases must be selected to match syllabus and curriculum requirements
constraints: Implemented with small cohorts (22 students); the authors note fewer MPH students per semester limits generalisation
Daily-performance assessment differed between experimental and control groups, so grades are not fully comparable
target_learners: Master of Public Health (MPH) graduate students
target_learning_goals: Theoretical understanding of environment and health
Application of knowledge and innovative spirit
examples: Cases across five topic areas were posted pre-class; groups of 3–4 students analysed cases, produced slides, and reported in class
key_sources: Li You, Cao Liang, Zhang Huixia, Pang Weiyi, Sun Yan, Zhang Zhiyong. (2023). Application of flipped classroom combined with case-based learning in Introduction to Environmental Health Science. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2023.1264843

article_title: The effect of flipped classroom in multiple clinical skills training for clinical interns on Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCE).
citation: Zhang Weihao, Gu Jiaoyang, Li Fan, Feng Feifei, Chen Huiqiang, Xing Xiaowei, Liu Lan. (2021). The effect of flipped classroom in multiple clinical skills training for clinical interns on Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCE). Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2021.2013405
title: Flipped classroom course structure for clinical skills training: pre-class videos plus weekly interactive offline sessions
description: The FC arm combined five online pre-class video sessions (55-minute physical examination videos and a 7-minute CPR video distributed on USB) with five weekly 45-minute offline sessions. In each offline session, a student group presented a randomly assigned PPT report, followed by "group discussion time was 15 minutes, the review time was 10 minutes", with teacher answers and summary of key points. Offline clinical skills teaching (20 minutes teacher demonstration, 25 minutes student practice) followed, matched to the TC arm in time, frequency, and content.
requirements: Students must complete online videos before the offline course
Identical offline teaching time, frequency, and content across comparison groups
Groups randomly formed for presentations
constraints: Videos were distributed on USB flash disks, so viewing habits and completion could not be verified beyond questionnaire self-report
examples: Offline FC sessions were held every Monday for a total of five times, with the presentation sequence and content randomly assigned.
key_sources: Zhang Weihao, Gu Jiaoyang, Li Fan, Feng Feifei, Chen Huiqiang, Xing Xiaowei, Liu Lan. (2021). The effect of flipped classroom in multiple clinical skills training for clinical interns on Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCE). Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2021.2013405

article_title: Implementation of flipped classroom combined with case-based learning: A promising and effective teaching modality in undergraduate pathology education.
citation: Cai L, Li Yl, Hu Xy, Li R, Khoshnood A. (2022). Implementation of flipped classroom combined with case-based learning: a promising and effective teaching modality in undergraduate pathology education. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000028782
title: Flipped classroom with case-based learning session structure for undergraduate pathology
description: A lesson-level design in which students study preprovided materials (learning purposes, annotated PowerPoints, web-based video lectures, typical case handouts) one week before class, prepare their own PPTs, then in pre-assigned groups of 7–8 present, discuss real clinical cases not disclosed until class, and receive instructor guidance and summary. The article states students "collaborated to take turns interpreting and discussing the real clinical cases proposed by instructors."
requirements: Preprovided course materials on the course website one week before class
Pre-assigned small groups (n = 7–8)
The same instructor and consistent content across compared formats
constraints: The article notes FC "consumes generous human, material and financial resources," including more faculty time preparing videos, PPTs and cases; only 2 textbook sections were implemented in this pilot
target_learners: third-year undergraduate medical students majoring in clinical medicine
target_learning_goals: understanding functional and structural changes of disease
clinical case analysis and higher-order cognitive abilities
examples: Two pathology textbook sections (cardiovascular and respiratory system diseases) were taught over 12 class hours following this structure, with post-class quizzes and Likert questionnaires as evaluation
key_sources: Cai L, Li Yl, Hu Xy, Li R, Khoshnood A. (2022). Implementation of flipped classroom combined with case-based learning: a promising and effective teaching modality in undergraduate pathology education. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000028782

article_title: Effects of a quasi-experimental study of using flipped classroom approach to teach evidence-based medicine to medical technology students.
citation: Huang Hsien-Li, Chou Chia-Pei, Leu Steve, You Huey-Ling, Tiao Mao-Meng, Chen Chih-Hung. (2020). Effects of a quasi-experimental study of using flipped classroom approach to teach evidence-based medicine to medical technology students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-1946-7
title: Tailor-made flipped-classroom EBM course for medical technology interns (FC-EBM)
description: A six-session flipped-classroom EBM course for medical technology interns, combining online self-study with in-class case discussion. "Seven eBook learning units" covered introduction to EBM through clinical use, each with "unit reading time was less than 15 min", and three clinical cases were discussed about 30 min per session. Class preparation included a learning platform, course description, counseling mechanism and information gathering.
requirements: Access to an online learning platform hosting the eBook and video materials; students study eBook and video material before class
constraints: Designed for medical technology interns with no prior EBM experience, focused on laboratory diagnosis problems such as reducing the hemolysis rate
target_learning_goals: evidence-based medicine competence: asking PICO questions, searching evidence, critical appraisal, clinical application
examples: Groups of 2–3 students discussed four study cases (e.g. whether compression socks prevent deep vein thrombosis); the traditional course used groups of 4–5 with standard lectures and after-class problem sets
key_sources: Huang Hsien-Li, Chou Chia-Pei, Leu Steve, You Huey-Ling, Tiao Mao-Meng, Chen Chih-Hung. (2020). Effects of a quasi-experimental study of using flipped classroom approach to teach evidence-based medicine to medical technology students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-1946-7

article_title: Effectiveness of flipped classroom combined with team-, case-, lecture- and evidence-based learning on ophthalmology teaching for eight-year program students.
citation: Ding Chun, Li Shengguo, Chen Baihua. (2019). Effectiveness of flipped classroom combined with team-, case-, lecture- and evidence-based learning on ophthalmology teaching for eight-year program students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1861-y
title: FC-TCLEBL: flipped classroom combined with team-, case-, lecture- and evidence-based learning for ophthalmology teaching
description: FC-TCLEBL is a self-designed ophthalmology teaching model that combines a flipped classroom with team-, case-, lecture- and evidence-based learning. Students study pre-class materials (PPTs, teaching videos, classic cases) shared via QQ or WeChat, work in four small teams preparing PowerPoint presentations on assigned subtopics of a diabetic retinopathy case, present in class, and the teacher recaps key points and summarizes evidence-based medicine sources. The article reports it aims to "promote student participation and strengthen the students' understanding of medical knowledge, clinical thinking, and scientific research while effectively reducing the students' extra-curricular burden."
requirements: Students need pre-class access to shared materials and internet resources, WeChat groups for teacher support, and organization into small teams with assigned presentation topics
constraints: The article's implementation was limited to a single chapter on diabetic retinopathy and did not address how to choose themes or frequency of use
The study did not compare the effects of FC, TBL and CBL separately
target_learners: eight-year medical program students in ophthalmology
examples: Students in four subgroups each presented clinical manifestations, anatomy and pathogenesis, diagnosis and differential diagnosis, or prevention and treatment of the disease
key_sources: Ding Chun, Li Shengguo, Chen Baihua. (2019). Effectiveness of flipped classroom combined with team-, case-, lecture- and evidence-based learning on ophthalmology teaching for eight-year program students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1861-y
